payload.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command (SQL Injection)
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-89 | Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command (SQL Injection)
The software builds an SQL command from user-controllable input without neutralising elements that could alter the command structure. An attacker who controls part of the query can read or modify data beyond their authorisation, and in some configurations execute operating system commands through database features. Typical payload markers include a quote that terminates a literal, a boolean tautology such as OR 1=1, a UNION SELECT that appends attacker-chosen columns, or a comment sequence that truncates the remainder of the statement. The reliable mitigation is parameterised queries or prepared statements, so that user input is always bound as data and never concatenated into the command text. Input validation and stored procedures help but do not substitute for parameterisation, and the database account used by the application should hold only the privileges it needs.

payload.title: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Cross-site Scripting)
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-79 | Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (Cross-site Scripting)
The software places user-controllable input into a web page without neutralising it for the output context, allowing script to execute in another user's browser. Variants are reflected, where the payload travels in the request, stored, where it is persisted and served to later visitors, and DOM-based, where client-side code writes untrusted data into the document. Consequences include session token theft, action forgery in the victim's session and defacement. The primary control is context-aware output encoding at the point of rendering, supported by a restrictive Content-Security-Policy and by setting HttpOnly and Secure flags on session cookies. Common payload markers include script tags, javascript URIs and event handler attributes such as onerror or onload.

payload.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command (OS Command Injection)
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-78 | Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command (OS Command Injection)
The software constructs an operating system command from externally influenced input without neutralising shell metacharacters. Successful injection typically yields execution with the privileges of the application process, which is often more than the application itself requires. The preferred mitigation is to avoid the shell entirely by invoking programs with an argument array, and failing that to apply strict allowlisting of permitted values. Semicolons, pipes, backticks and command substitution sequences in a parameter that reaches a command are the characteristic indicators.

payload.title: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory (Path Traversal)
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-22 | Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory (Path Traversal)
The software uses external input to construct a pathname without properly neutralising sequences that resolve outside the intended directory. Attackers use relative traversal sequences, sometimes encoded, to read configuration files, credentials or application source. Mitigation is to canonicalise the resolved path and verify that it remains within an approved base directory, rather than filtering traversal strings.

payload.title: Improper Authentication
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-287 | Improper Authentication
The software does not adequately prove that a claimed identity is correct, allowing an actor to act as another user. Instances include accepting unverified identity assertions, flawed session handling and logic that can be bypassed by manipulating request parameters. Because authentication is the boundary on which authorisation depends, defects here typically have high impact. Mitigation includes using a vetted authentication framework, verifying assertions server side, and adding multi-factor authentication for sensitive access.

payload.title: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-307 | Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
The software permits an unlimited or insufficiently limited number of authentication attempts, which makes password guessing and credential stuffing practical. The weakness is the direct enabler of brute-force attacks against an exposed login interface. Mitigations include progressive delays, temporary account lockout, per-source rate limiting and challenge mechanisms after repeated failures. Lockout policy must be balanced against the denial-of-service risk of allowing an attacker to lock legitimate users out deliberately, which is one reason throttling and multi-factor authentication are often preferred to hard lockout.

payload.title: Weak Password Requirements
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-521 | Weak Password Requirements
The product does not require users to choose passwords that resist guessing, so credentials fall quickly to dictionary and brute-force attempts. Modern guidance favours a substantial minimum length and screening candidate passwords against lists of known-breached values, rather than mandating composition rules and frequent rotation. Weak password requirements amplify the impact of any missing rate limiting.

payload.title: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-798 | Use of Hard-coded Credentials
The product contains credentials embedded in source code, configuration or firmware. Anyone who can read the artefact obtains the credential, and rotation requires a code change, so the secret tends to persist for years and to be shared across deployments. Mitigation is to load secrets from a managed secret store or environment configuration at runtime, to scan repositories for committed secrets, and to rotate any credential that has ever been committed.

payload.title: Improper Privilege Management
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-269 | Improper Privilege Management
The software does not correctly assign, track or revoke privileges, allowing an actor to gain rights beyond those intended. Instances include failing to drop privileges after a privileged operation, granting broad roles by default, and not revoking access when a role changes. Regular entitlement review and least-privilege defaults are the practical mitigations, and any unexplained privilege change should be treated as a potential escalation event.

payload.title: Execution with Unnecessary Privileges
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-250 | Execution with Unnecessary Privileges
The software runs with more privilege than its function requires, so any defect it contains becomes more damaging. Services running as root or as a domain administrator are the classic case. Mitigation is to run each component under a dedicated least-privilege account and to drop elevated rights immediately after any operation that genuinely needs them.

payload.title: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-200 | Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
The product discloses information to an actor not explicitly authorised to have it. Disclosure may be direct, such as returning another user's record, or indirect, such as verbose error messages and debug endpoints that reveal internal structure. Exposure often precedes a larger intrusion because it supplies the attacker with the details needed for a targeted attack. Controls include authorisation checks on every retrieval path and suppressing internal detail in error responses.

payload.title: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-311 | Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data
The software does not encrypt sensitive data in transit or at rest, so anyone with access to the channel or the storage medium can read it. The weakness converts an otherwise limited access event into a full data disclosure. Mitigation is to apply transport encryption for all sensitive traffic and to encrypt sensitive fields or volumes at rest with managed keys.

payload.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-352 | Cross-Site Request Forgery
The application performs a state-changing request without verifying that the request was intentionally submitted by the authenticated user. An attacker can therefore cause actions to occur in a victim's session simply by inducing the victim to load a crafted page. Mitigation is to require an unpredictable per-session token on state-changing requests and to set SameSite attributes on session cookies.

payload.title: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-434 | Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
The software permits upload of files that can be executed or interpreted by the server environment. When an uploaded file lands in a location that the web server will execute, the result is direct remote code execution. Mitigation is to store uploads outside the web root, to validate type by content rather than extension, to rewrite file names, and to serve uploads from a domain with no execution capability.

payload.title: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-400 | Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
The software does not properly limit the resources an actor can consume, permitting denial of service with relatively little attacker effort. Unbounded request sizes, unlimited concurrent connections and expensive operations reachable without authentication are common causes. Mitigation is explicit quotas, timeouts and back-pressure at every entry point.

payload.title: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
payload.content:
CWE | CWE-770 | Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
The software allocates a reusable resource without limiting how much a single actor may hold, allowing exhaustion of memory, connections, threads or storage. This weakness underlies many application-layer denial-of-service conditions where traffic volume is modest but resource cost per request is high. Mitigation is per-client throttling, connection and memory caps, and rejecting work once a saturation threshold is reached.

payload.title: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide: incident response life cycle
payload.content:
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 | SP800-61-lifecycle | Computer Security Incident Handling Guide: incident response life cycle
The incident response life cycle has four phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. Preparation establishes the capability before an incident occurs, including tooling, contacts and communication plans. Detection and analysis determines whether an incident has occurred, its scope and its impact, and requires correlating evidence from several sources because a single indicator is rarely conclusive. Containment decisions balance stopping the damage against preserving evidence and maintaining service, and organisations should decide containment strategy in advance for each incident type rather than during the event. Post-incident review converts the event into improved detection and prevention.

payload.title: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide: evidence handling and prioritisation
payload.content:
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 | SP800-61-evidence | Computer Security Incident Handling Guide: evidence handling and prioritisation
Incidents should be prioritised by functional impact, information impact and recoverability rather than handled first-in first-out. Evidence should be collected according to documented procedures with a maintained chain of custody, because containment actions frequently destroy volatile evidence. Detailed records of every action taken, with timestamps, support both the investigation and any subsequent legal process. Handlers should preserve volatile data such as memory and active network connections before shutting down or reimaging an affected system.

payload.title: Digital Identity Guidelines: authentication and lifecycle management
payload.content:
NIST SP 800-63B | SP800-63B-auth | Digital Identity Guidelines: authentication and lifecycle management
Verifiers should compare prospective passwords against lists of values known to be commonly used or compromised, and should not impose composition rules or arbitrary periodic rotation, which drive predictable user behaviour. Rate limiting must be applied to defend against online guessing, with a limited number of consecutive failed attempts per account. Multi-factor authentication substantially reduces the value of a stolen or guessed password, and phishing-resistant authenticators offer the strongest protection against credential interception. Passwords should be salted and hashed with a memory-hard function before storage.

payload.title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
payload.content:
OWASP | OWASP-SQLI-CS | SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
The primary defence against SQL injection is the use of prepared statements with parameterised queries, which keep user input as bound data that can never alter query structure. Where parameterisation is impossible, such as for dynamic table or column names, use a strict allowlist of permitted values. Secondary defences include applying least privilege to the database account and validating input, but neither replaces parameterisation. Escaping user input by hand is error prone and should be a last resort.

payload.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
payload.content:
OWASP | OWASP-XSS-CS | Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
Prevent cross-site scripting by encoding untrusted data for the specific context in which it is rendered, since the rules for HTML body, attributes, JavaScript and URLs differ. Prefer frameworks that encode by default and avoid sinks that write raw markup into the document. A Content-Security-Policy provides defence in depth by restricting which scripts may execute, and HttpOnly cookies limit the value of a successful payload. Where user-supplied HTML must be permitted, sanitise it with a maintained library rather than a custom filter.

payload.title: OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks
payload.content:
OWASP | OWASP-TOP10 | OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks
The OWASP Top 10 is a consensus document describing the most critical categories of web application security risk, used widely as an awareness and baseline assurance reference. Categories include broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, security misconfiguration, vulnerable and outdated components, identification and authentication failures, software and data integrity failures, security logging and monitoring failures, and server-side request forgery. Injection covers SQL, command and similar defects where untrusted input is interpreted as part of a command. Logging and monitoring failures are included because undetected breaches persist far longer and cost substantially more to resolve.

payload.title: Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks
payload.content:
CISA | CISA-PHISHING | Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks
Social engineering attacks manipulate a person into disclosing information or taking an action rather than exploiting a technical defect. Recipients should be suspicious of unsolicited messages that create urgency, request credentials, or ask them to follow a link to verify an account. Verifying the request through an independently known contact route, rather than the details supplied in the message, defeats most such attempts. Organisations should provide a simple mechanism for staff to report suspicious messages, since early reporting enables the whole campaign to be scoped and removed.

payload.title: Understanding and Responding to Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks
payload.content:
CISA | CISA-DDOS | Understanding and Responding to Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks
A distributed denial-of-service attack uses many sources to exhaust the capacity of a target service or its network path. Preparation matters more than reaction: organisations should understand their normal traffic profile, know their provider's mitigation options, and hold contacts ready before an event. During an attack, characterise the traffic and engage the upstream provider or a scrubbing service, because saturation of the inbound link cannot be mitigated at the far end. Rate limiting and geographic or protocol filtering can preserve capacity for legitimate users, and service degradation should be planned so that critical functions survive.

payload.title: Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops
payload.content:
NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1 | SP800-83-malware | Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops
Malware incident handling combines prevention through patching, least privilege and application restriction with detection through endpoint and network monitoring. Containment should consider the trade-off between isolating a host quickly and preserving volatile evidence needed to understand the intrusion. Identification of the specific malware and its indicators enables the estate to be searched for other affected hosts before eradication begins. Recovery should restore from known-good media or backups, because cleaning in place cannot guarantee the removal of persistence mechanisms.

payload.title: Using ATT&CK for threat-informed analysis
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | ATTACK-METHODOLOGY | Using ATT&CK for threat-informed analysis
ATT&CK is a curated knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques observed in real intrusions, organised so that tactics represent the adversary objective and techniques the means of achieving it. Mapping observed activity to techniques supports consistent communication, gap analysis of detection coverage, and reasoning about what an adversary is likely to do next. A mapping should be asserted only where the available evidence supports it; speculative mapping inflates apparent confidence and misleads later analysis. Because a single observation often fits several techniques, analysts should record the evidence that justified the chosen mapping.

payload.title: Active Scanning
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1595 | Active Scanning | tactic: Reconnaissance
Adversaries probe victim infrastructure with active network traffic before an intrusion, in contrast to passive collection of public information. Scanning reveals which hosts are reachable, which services listen on which ports, and which software versions are exposed. The traffic is directed at the target rather than at a third-party dataset, so it is visible in perimeter firewall, IDS and web server logs. Detection focuses on connection attempts across many ports or addresses from a single source in a short window. Scanning alone is not an intrusion, but it frequently precedes exploitation attempts against the services it discovers.

payload.title: Active Scanning: Scanning IP Blocks
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1595.001 | Active Scanning: Scanning IP Blocks | tactic: Reconnaissance
Adversaries sweep ranges of IP addresses to learn which addresses are in use and which respond. Techniques include ICMP echo sweeps and TCP or UDP connection attempts across a contiguous address block. The resulting map of live hosts guides later, more targeted scanning. In logs this appears as a single source contacting many sequential addresses within one subnet.

payload.title: Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1595.002 | Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning | tactic: Reconnaissance
Adversaries check exposed services for configurations and software versions known to be vulnerable. Scanners commonly fingerprint banners, request known paths, or send probe payloads that reveal whether a defect is present without fully exploiting it. Web server logs often show bursts of requests to unusual paths, and identifiable scanner user-agent strings may be present. A vulnerability scan against an internet-facing service is a strong precursor signal for an exploitation attempt.

payload.title: Network Service Discovery
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1046 | Network Service Discovery | tactic: Discovery
Adversaries enumerate services running on remote hosts, usually after they already have some access to the network. Port scanning from an internal host is a common form and is more significant than external scanning because it indicates a foothold already exists. Detection relies on internal flow records showing a workstation contacting many peers or many ports, which is unusual for normal endpoint behaviour. This activity often bridges initial access and lateral movement.

payload.title: Account Discovery
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1087 | Account Discovery | tactic: Discovery
Adversaries enumerate local, domain or cloud accounts to identify targets for credential access and privilege escalation. Enumeration may use built-in operating system utilities, directory service queries, or cloud provider APIs. Because the same commands are used by administrators, detection depends on context such as the account performing the query and whether it normally does so.

payload.title: Phishing
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1566 | Phishing | tactic: Initial Access
Adversaries send fraudulent messages to obtain credentials or to induce execution of malicious content. Phishing may be broad and untargeted or narrowly tailored to an individual or role, which is known as spearphishing. Messages commonly impersonate a trusted brand or colleague, create urgency, and direct the recipient to a credential-harvesting page or an attachment. Analysis should preserve full message headers, because the visible display name is trivially forged while the delivery path and authentication results are not. Failed SPF, DKIM or DMARC checks, a reply-to address differing from the sender, and a recently registered link domain are all supporting indicators.

payload.title: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1566.001 | Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment | tactic: Initial Access
Adversaries attach a malicious file to a targeted email and rely on the recipient opening it. Common carriers include office documents with macros, archive files containing scripts or shortcuts, and installers disguised as invoices or reports. Execution usually requires the user to bypass a security warning, so awareness controls and macro restrictions materially reduce success. Mail gateway logs and endpoint process trees showing an office application spawning a script interpreter are primary detection sources.

payload.title: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1566.002 | Phishing: Spearphishing Link | tactic: Initial Access
Adversaries include a link in a targeted email rather than an attachment, so no malicious file traverses the mail gateway. The linked page typically imitates a familiar login portal to harvest credentials, or delivers a payload on visit. Indicators include a display text that does not match the underlying href, a lookalike or newly registered domain, and URL shorteners that hide the destination. Investigation should determine not only who received the message but who clicked and who submitted credentials.

payload.title: Exploit Public-Facing Application
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1190 | Exploit Public-Facing Application | tactic: Initial Access
Adversaries exploit a weakness in an internet-facing application to gain access to the host or the data behind it. Common classes include injection defects, deserialisation flaws, authentication bypasses and file upload weaknesses. Web application and database logs frequently contain the payload itself, which makes them the primary evidence source. Reducing exposed surface, patching promptly and running applications with least privilege limit both the likelihood and the impact of this technique.

payload.title: Valid Accounts
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1078 | Valid Accounts | tactic: Initial Access
Adversaries use legitimate credentials to access systems, which makes their activity blend with normal operations. Valid accounts support initial access, persistence, privilege escalation and defence evasion simultaneously, because authorised sessions bypass many detections. Signals of misuse are contextual rather than signature based: sign-in from an unfamiliar location or device, access at an unusual time, or activity inconsistent with the account role. Multi-factor authentication and conditional access substantially raise the cost of this technique.

payload.title: External Remote Services
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1133 | External Remote Services | tactic: Initial Access
Adversaries abuse externally reachable remote access services such as VPN concentrators, remote desktop gateways and management interfaces. These services accept authentication from the internet by design, so exposed instances attract both credential guessing and exploitation. Restricting access to known networks, enforcing multi-factor authentication and monitoring authentication volume are the principal controls.

payload.title: User Execution
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1204 | User Execution | tactic: Execution
Adversaries rely on a user taking an action that runs malicious code, such as opening a file or following a link. The technique depends on social engineering rather than a software defect, so patching does not remove it. Endpoint telemetry showing a document, browser or mail client spawning a script interpreter or unexpected binary is the strongest detection signal.

payload.title: User Execution: Malicious Link
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1204.001 | User Execution: Malicious Link | tactic: Execution
A user follows an adversary-supplied link that leads to code execution or credential capture. This step usually follows a phishing message and precedes credential access or payload delivery. Proxy and DNS logs establish whether the link was actually visited, which distinguishes an attempted campaign from a successful one.

payload.title: User Execution: Malicious File
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1204.002 | User Execution: Malicious File | tactic: Execution
A user opens an adversary-supplied file that executes code, commonly a document with macros, a script, a shortcut file or a disguised executable. The file hash and the resulting process tree are the core artefacts for scoping the intrusion. Searching the estate for the same hash reveals other recipients who may already have executed it.

payload.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1059 | Command and Scripting Interpreter | tactic: Execution
Adversaries execute commands through interpreters such as PowerShell, Windows command shell, Unix shells, or scripting runtimes. Because interpreters are legitimate and preinstalled, the technique supports living-off-the-land operations with no additional tooling. Detection depends on command-line logging and script block logging rather than file signatures, and on identifying encoded or obfuscated arguments.

payload.title: Brute Force
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1110 | Brute Force | tactic: Credential Access
Adversaries attempt to obtain credentials by systematically guessing them when they have no prior knowledge of the password. The characteristic signal is a high volume of authentication failures concentrated on one account, one source, or one service within a short interval. A successful authentication immediately following a burst of failures from the same source is a strong indicator of compromise and should be treated as such until disproved. Effective controls include account lockout or throttling, rate limiting at the network edge, multi-factor authentication, and monitoring for authentication failure spikes. Investigation should always determine whether any attempt succeeded, not merely that attempts occurred.

payload.title: Brute Force: Password Guessing
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1110.001 | Brute Force: Password Guessing | tactic: Credential Access
Adversaries guess many passwords against one account without prior knowledge of the credential. Guesses often come from common password lists or from information about the target. The pattern is many failures for a single username, which account lockout policies are specifically designed to interrupt.

payload.title: Brute Force: Password Spraying
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1110.003 | Brute Force: Password Spraying | tactic: Credential Access
Adversaries try a small number of commonly used passwords against many accounts, deliberately staying below lockout thresholds. Because failures are spread thinly across accounts, per-account monitoring misses the pattern entirely. Detection requires aggregation across the directory, looking for one source producing single failures against many distinct usernames.

payload.title: Brute Force: Credential Stuffing
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1110.004 | Brute Force: Credential Stuffing | tactic: Credential Access
Adversaries replay username and password pairs stolen from unrelated breaches, exploiting password reuse. Success rates per attempt are low but the volume is high and the credentials are valid somewhere, so a proportion of attempts succeed outright. Indicators include distributed sources, high request volume against the login endpoint, and successful logins from addresses with no prior history for that account.

payload.title: OS Credential Dumping
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1003 | OS Credential Dumping | tactic: Credential Access
Adversaries extract credential material such as password hashes or plaintext secrets from operating system memory and credential stores. On Windows this frequently involves access to the LSASS process or to the SAM and NTDS databases. Successful dumping typically converts a single compromised host into estate-wide access, so it is a high-impact event. Detection focuses on unusual process access to credential stores and on known tooling behaviour rather than on file names.

payload.title: Credentials from Password Stores
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1555 | Credentials from Password Stores | tactic: Credential Access
Adversaries retrieve credentials saved in browsers, password managers and operating system keychains. These stores concentrate high-value secrets in predictable locations, which makes them efficient targets after initial access. Monitoring for processes reading browser credential databases, and requiring re-authentication for vault access, are the practical controls.

payload.title: Unsecured Credentials
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1552 | Unsecured Credentials | tactic: Credential Access
Adversaries search for credentials stored insecurely in configuration files, scripts, source code repositories, command histories and cloud instance metadata. No exploitation is required because the secret is simply readable. Prevention relies on secret management systems, pre-commit scanning and rotating any credential that has ever been written to a file or a log.

payload.title: Input Capture
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1056 | Input Capture | tactic: Credential Access
Adversaries capture user input to obtain credentials, using keylogging, credential prompts that imitate legitimate dialogs, or interception of web forms. Captured input yields credentials that no password policy can protect. Detection focuses on unexpected hooks into input APIs and on unauthorised software installation.

payload.title: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1068 | Exploitation for Privilege Escalation | tactic: Privilege Escalation
Adversaries exploit a software defect to obtain higher privileges on a system they already have access to. Kernel drivers and privileged services are the usual targets because they run with elevated rights. Successful escalation invalidates host-level containment assumptions and should raise incident severity. Patching, exploit mitigations and least-privilege service accounts are the primary defences.

payload.title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1548 | Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism | tactic: Privilege Escalation
Adversaries bypass or abuse the mechanisms intended to control elevation, such as user account control, sudo configuration or setuid binaries. No software defect is necessarily required; misconfiguration is often sufficient. Auditing sudo rules and elevation prompts, and alerting on privilege changes, are the practical controls.

payload.title: Access Token Manipulation
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1134 | Access Token Manipulation | tactic: Privilege Escalation
Adversaries manipulate access tokens to run processes under a different security context than the one they authenticated with. This both escalates privilege and confuses attribution, because subsequent actions appear to belong to another account. Detection depends on process-level auditing of token operations rather than on authentication logs.

payload.title: Scheduled Task/Job
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1053 | Scheduled Task/Job | tactic: Persistence
Adversaries schedule tasks or jobs to run code at a chosen time or on system start, providing persistence and sometimes privilege escalation. The mechanism is legitimate and widely used by administrators, so detection depends on baselining which tasks should exist. Newly created tasks that invoke script interpreters or write to unusual paths deserve investigation.

payload.title: Create Account
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1136 | Create Account | tactic: Persistence
Adversaries create local, domain or cloud accounts to retain access independently of any credential the defender may reset. An account created outside the normal provisioning process is a high-fidelity indicator, because legitimate account creation almost always has a corresponding ticket or workflow record. Reviewing recently created accounts is a standard step when scoping an intrusion.

payload.title: Indicator Removal
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1070 | Indicator Removal | tactic: Defense Evasion
Adversaries delete or alter logs, command histories and files to hinder detection and investigation. Cleared event logs and truncated histories are themselves evidence, because legitimate operations rarely produce them. Forwarding logs to a separate system that the compromised host cannot modify is the effective countermeasure.

payload.title: Obfuscated Files or Information
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1027 | Obfuscated Files or Information | tactic: Defense Evasion
Adversaries encode, encrypt, pack or otherwise obscure payloads and commands to defeat signature-based inspection. Base64-encoded command lines, packed binaries and password-protected archives are common forms. Detection shifts from content signatures to behavioural indicators such as an interpreter decoding a long argument at runtime.

payload.title: Data from Information Repositories
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1213 | Data from Information Repositories | tactic: Collection
Adversaries mine internal repositories such as wikis, ticketing systems, code repositories and file shares for valuable data and for credentials embedded in documentation. Access is often through legitimate accounts, so volume and breadth of access are the discriminating signals. Bulk retrieval outside a user role is a common insider-threat indicator as well.

payload.title: Data from Local System
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1005 | Data from Local System | tactic: Collection
Adversaries gather files and data from a compromised host prior to exfiltration, often staging them into a single archive first. The appearance of a large archive in a temporary directory shortly before outbound transfer is a recognisable staging pattern. Correlating collection with a subsequent transfer establishes the exfiltration sequence.

payload.title: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1041 | Exfiltration Over C2 Channel | tactic: Exfiltration
Adversaries send collected data out over the same channel already used for command and control, avoiding a second, separately detectable connection. Detection focuses on the ratio of outbound to inbound bytes on a session, on beaconing regularity, and on destinations with no business relationship. Network flow records rather than payload inspection usually provide the evidence.

payload.title: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1048 | Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol | tactic: Exfiltration
Adversaries move data out using a protocol different from the command-and-control channel, such as DNS, FTP or SMTP. Protocol misuse of this kind often evades controls tuned only to web traffic. Unusually large or frequent DNS queries with encoded subdomains are a classic indicator.

payload.title: Exfiltration Over Web Service
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1567 | Exfiltration Over Web Service | tactic: Exfiltration
Adversaries upload data to legitimate cloud storage, code hosting or paste services, so the destination is a reputable domain that blocklists will not catch. The traffic is encrypted and indistinguishable from normal use of the same service. Controls rely on data loss prevention, on restricting unsanctioned services, and on alerting when upload volume for an account departs from its baseline.

payload.title: Data Transfer Size Limits
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1030 | Data Transfer Size Limits | tactic: Exfiltration
Adversaries split exfiltrated data into small chunks to stay under volume-based alerting thresholds. Because no single transfer looks anomalous, detection requires aggregating transfer volume per host or account over a longer window. Regular, similarly sized outbound transfers to one destination are the pattern to look for.

payload.title: Network Denial of Service
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1498 | Network Denial of Service | tactic: Impact
Adversaries exhaust network bandwidth or infrastructure capacity to make a service unavailable to legitimate users. Volumetric floods and reflection or amplification attacks are the common forms, and traffic frequently originates from many distributed sources. Because saturation occurs upstream of the target, effective mitigation requires cooperation with the network provider or a scrubbing service rather than local filtering alone. Characterising the traffic by protocol, source distribution and request pattern is the first response step.

payload.title: Endpoint Denial of Service
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1499 | Endpoint Denial of Service | tactic: Impact
Adversaries exhaust the resources of a specific service or application rather than the network link, for example by consuming connection tables, worker threads or application state. Attack volume can be modest while still being effective, which distinguishes it from volumetric flooding. Rate limiting, connection timeouts and resource quotas at the application layer are the relevant controls.

payload.title: Data Encrypted for Impact
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1486 | Data Encrypted for Impact | tactic: Impact
Adversaries encrypt data in place to deny access to it, which is the defining behaviour of ransomware. Encryption is usually preceded by credential theft, lateral movement and deliberate destruction of backups and shadow copies. Detection signals include mass file modification, rapid entropy change across a share, and deletion of recovery points. Tested offline backups remain the control that most reliably determines the outcome.

payload.title: Data Destruction
payload.content:
MITRE ATT&CK | T1485 | Data Destruction | tactic: Impact
Adversaries irrecoverably delete or overwrite files and storage to disrupt operations, sometimes to destroy evidence of prior activity. Unlike ransomware there is no recovery path through payment, so backup integrity is the only remedy. Mass deletion events and use of secure-wipe utilities are the detection signals.
